passages.passageHtml:
It was at the end of the discussion that Mr. Wickson spoke. He was the only one that was cool, and Ernest treated him with a respect he had not accorded the others.

"No answer is necessary," Mr. Wickson said with slow deliberation. "I have followed the whole discussion with amazement and disgust. I am disgusted with you gentlemen, members of my class. You have behaved like foolish little schoolboys, what with intruding ethics and the thunder of the common politician into such a discussion. You have been outgeneralled and outclassed. You have been very wordy, and all you have done is buzz. You have buzzed like gnats about a bear. Gentlemen, there stands the bear" (he pointed at Ernest), "and your buzzing has only tickled his ears.

"Believe me, the situation is serious. That bear reached out his paws tonight to crush us. He has said there are a million and a half of revolutionists in the United States. That is a fact. He has said that it is their intention to take away from us our governments, our palaces, and all our purpled ease. That, also, is a fact. A change, a great change, is coming in society; but, haply, it may not be the change the bear anticipates. The bear has said that he will crush us. What if we crush the bear?"

The throat-rumble arose in the great room, and man nodded to man with indorsement and certitude. Their faces were set hard. They were fighters, that was certain.

"But not by buzzing will we crush the bear," Mr. Wickson went on coldly and dispassionately. "We will hunt the bear. We will not reply to the bear in words. Our reply shall be couched in terms of lead. We are in power. Nobody will deny it. By virtue of that power we shall remain in power."

He turned suddenly upon Ernest. The moment was dramatic.

"This, then, is our answer. We have no words to waste on you. When you reach out your vaunted strong hands for our palaces and purpled ease, we will show you what strength is. In roar of shell and shrapnel and in whine of machine-guns will our answer be couched. We will grind you revolutionists down under our heel, and we shall walk upon your faces. The world is ours, we are its lords, and ours it shall remain. As for the host of labor, it has been in the dirt since history began, and I read history aright. And in the dirt it shall remain so long as I and mine and those that come after us have the power. There is the word. It is the king of words—Power. Not God, not Mammon, but Power. Pour it over your tongue till it tingles with it. Power."

"I am answered," Ernest said quietly. "It is the only answer that could be given. Power. It is what we of the working class preach. We know, and well we know by bitter experience, that no appeal for the right, for justice, for humanity, can ever touch you. Your hearts are hard as your heels with which you tread upon the faces of the poor. So we have preached power. By the power of our ballots on election day will we take your government away from you—"

"My theory is, that my interests are identical with those of my workpeople, and vice- versa. ... In our infancy we require a wise despotism to govern us. ... I agree with Miss Hale so far as to consider our people in the condition of children, while I deny that we, the masters, have anything to do with the making or keeping them so. I maintain that despotism is the best kind of government for them; so that in the hours in which I come in contact with them I must necessarily be an autocrat. ... Let them turn out! I shall suffer as well as they: but in the end they will find I have not bated nor altered one jot."

Margaret had re-entered the room... "Very lately," said Margaret, "I heard a story of what happened in Nuremberg ... A rich man ... had a son—an overgrown man, with the unexercised intellect of a child, whom he had kept up in that strange way, in order to save him from temptation and error. ... His father had made the blunder of bringing him up in ignorance and taking it for innocence..."

"I used the comparison ... of the position of the master to that of a parent ... But, Mr. Hale, when you were setting up a wise parent as a model for us, you said he humoured his children ... I value my own independence so highly that I can fancy no degradation greater than that of having another man perpetually directing and advising and lecturing me..."

"But," said Margaret in a low voice, "it seems to me that it makes all the difference in the world—" Her father made a sign to her to be silent...

"You must grant me this one point. Given a strong feeling of independence in every Darkshire man, have I any right to obtrude my views ... merely because he has labour to sell and I capital to buy?"

"Not in the least," said Margaret, "... but because you are a man, dealing with a set of men over whom you have ... immense power, just because your lives and your welfare are so constantly and intimately interwoven."

"Just tell me, Miss Hale, are you yourself ever conscious of being influenced by others ... Have they been labouring to exhort ... or have they been simple, true men, taking up their duty, and doing it unflinchingly ...? I rely on the straightforward honesty of my hands. ... What the master is, that will the men be."

"There was a time, when the earth was to all appearance utterly destitute both of animal and vegetable life, and when according to the opinion of our best philosophers it was simply a hot round ball with a crust gradually cooling. Now if a human being had existed while the earth was in this state and had been allowed to see it as though it were some other world with which he had no concern, and if at the same time he were entirely ignorant of all physical science, would he not have pronounced it impossible that creatures possessed of anything like consciousness should be evolved from the seeming cinder which he was beholding? Would he not have denied that it contained any potentiality of consciousness? Yet in the course of time consciousness came. Is it not possible then that there may be even yet new channels dug out for consciousness, though we can detect no signs of them at present?

"Again. Consciousness, in anything like the present acceptation of the term, having been once a new thing—a thing, as far as we can see, subsequent even to an individual centre of action and to a reproductive system (which we see existing in plants without apparent consciousness)—why may not there arise some new phase of mind which shall be as different from all present known phases, as the mind of animals is from that of vegetables?

"There is a kind of plant that eats organic food with its flowers: when a fly settles upon the blossom, the petals close upon it and hold it fast till the plant has absorbed the insect into its system; but they will close on nothing but what is good to eat; of a drop of rain or a piece of stick they will take no notice. Curious! that so unconscious a thing should have such a keen eye to its own interest. If this is unconsciousness, where is the use of consciousness?

"Shall we say that the plant does not know what it is doing merely because it has no eyes, or ears, or brains? If we say that it acts mechanically, and mechanically only, shall we not be forced to admit that sundry other and apparently very deliberate actions are also mechanical?...

"Even a potato in a dark cellar has a certain low cunning about him which serves him in excellent stead. He knows perfectly well what he wants and how to get it. He sees the light coming from the cellar window and sends his shoots crawling straight thereto... What deliberation he may exercise... is a thing unknown to us, but we can imagine him saying, 'I will have a tuber here and a tuber there, and I will suck whatsoever advantage I can from all my surroundings.'

"The potato says these things by doing them, which is the best of languages. What is consciousness if this is not consciousness?...

"If it be urged that the action of the potato is chemical and mechanical only... the answer would seem to lie in an inquiry whether every sensation is not chemical and mechanical in its operation? whether those things which we deem most purely spiritual are anything but disturbances of equilibrium in an infinite series of levers... whether there be not a molecular action of thought, whence a dynamical theory of the passions shall be deducible?"

"In general," I said, "what impresses me most about the city is the material prosperity on the part of the people which its magnificence implies."

"I would give a great deal for just one glimpse of the Boston of your day," replied Dr. Leete. "No doubt, as you imply, the cities of that period were rather shabby affairs. If you had the taste to make them splendid, which I would not be so rude as to question, the general poverty resulting from your extraordinary industrial system would not have given you the means. Moreover, the excessive individualism which then prevailed was inconsistent with much public spirit. What little wealth you had seems almost wholly to have been lavished in private luxury. Nowadays, on the contrary, there is no destination of the surplus wealth so popular as the adornment of the city, which all enjoy in equal degree."

The sun had been setting as we returned to the house-top, and as we talked night descended upon the city.

"It is growing dark," said Dr. Leete. "Let us descend into the house; I want to introduce my wife and daughter to you."

His words recalled to me the feminine voices which I had heard whispering about me as I was coming back to conscious life; and, most curious to learn what the ladies of the year 2000 were like, I assented with alacrity to the proposition. The apartment in which we found the wife and daughter of my host, as well as the entire interior of the house, was filled with a mellow light, which I knew must be artificial, although I could not discover the source from which it was diffused. Mrs. Leete was an exceptionally fine looking and well preserved woman of about her husband's age, while the daughter, who was in the first blush of womanhood, was the most beautiful girl I had ever seen. Her face was as bewitching as deep blue eyes, delicately tinted complexion, and perfect features could make it, but even had her countenance lacked special charms, the faultless luxuriance of her figure would have given her place as a beauty among the women of the nineteenth century. Feminine softness and delicacy were in this lovely creature deliciously combined with an appearance of health and abounding physical vitality too often lacking in the maidens with whom alone I could compare her.

[Footnote 1: In accounting for this state of mind it must be remembered that, except for the topic of our conversations, there was in my surroundings next to nothing to suggest what had befallen me. Within a block of my home in the old Boston I could have found social circles vastly more foreign to me. The speech of the Bostonians of the twentieth century differs even less from that of their cultured ancestors of the nineteenth than did that of the latter from the language of Washington and Franklin, while the differences between the style of dress and furniture of the two epochs are not more marked than I have known fashion to make in the time of one generation.]

Dr. Maynard, the well-known surgeon of Thirty-sixth Street, was the first witness called. His testimony concerned the nature of the wound found in the murdered man's head. As some of the facts presented by him are likely to prove of importance to us in our narrative, I will proceed to give a synopsis of what he said.

Prefacing his remarks with some account of himself, and the manner in which he had been summoned to the house by one of the servants, he went on to state that, upon his arrival, he found the deceased lying on a bed in the second-story front room, with the blood clotted about a pistol-wound in the back of the head; having evidently been carried there from the adjoining apartment some hours after death. It was the only wound discovered on the body, and having probed it, he had found and extracted the bullet which he now handed to the jury. It was lying in the brain, having entered at the base of the skull, passed obliquely upward, and at once struck the medulla oblongata, causing instant death. The fact of the ball having entered the brain in this peculiar manner he deemed worthy of note, since it would produce not only instantaneous death, but an utterly motionless one. Further, from the position of the bullet-hole and the direction taken by the bullet, it was manifestly impossible that the shot should have been fired by the man himself, even if the condition of the hair about the wound did not completely demonstrate the fact that the shot was fired from a point some three or four feet distant. Still further, considering the angle at which the bullet had entered the skull, it was evident that the deceased must not only have been seated at the time, a fact about which there could be no dispute, but he must also have been engaged in some occupation which drew his head forward. For, in order that a ball should enter the head of a man sitting erect at the angle seen here, of 45 degrees, it would be necessary, not only for the pistol to be held very low down, but in a peculiar position; while if the head had been bent forward, as in the act of writing, a man holding a pistol naturally with the elbow bent, might very easily fire a ball into the brain at the angle observed.

Upon being questioned in regard to the bodily health of Mr. Leavenworth, he replied that the deceased appeared to have been in good condition at the time of his death, but that, not being his attendant physician, he could not speak conclusively upon the subject without further examination; and, to the remark of a juryman, observed that he had not seen pistol or weapon lying upon the floor, or, indeed, anywhere else in either of the above-mentioned rooms.

I might as well add here what he afterwards stated, that from the position of the table, the chair, and the door behind it, the murderer, in order to satisfy all the conditions imposed by the situation, must have stood upon, or just within, the threshold of the passageway leading into the room beyond. Also, that as the ball was small, and from a rifled barrel, and thus especially liable to deflections while passing through bones and integuments, it seemed to him evident that the victim had made no effort to raise or turn his head when advanced upon by his destroyer; the fearful conclusion being that the footstep was an accustomed one, and the presence of its possessor in the room either known or expected.

questions.questionHtml: Mr. Wickson says: "We will not reply to the bear in words. Our reply shall be couched in terms of lead." What conclusion about Mr. Wickson's view of political debate is best supported by the passage?

options.A: He believes that verbal arguments are worthless because the working class is incapable of understanding complex ideas.
options.B: He thinks that ethical appeals and political rhetoric are irrelevant when one side has already committed to using violence.
options.C: He rejects dialogue because he secretly fears that Ernest's logic is correct and cannot be refuted.
options.D: He argues that only direct physical action, not speeches, can ever change the distribution of wealth in society.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

Option A is incorrect. Nowhere does Wickson say that the working class is incapable of understanding complex ideas. He criticizes his own class members for using "ethics" and "thunder of the common politician," but he does not insult the intelligence of the revolutionists. The phrase "the bear" suggests Ernest is powerful, not stupid. This option misreads the text.

Option B is correct. Wickson explicitly dismisses "buzzing" (words, ethics, political rhetoric) as useless. He says "our reply shall be couched in terms of lead" (bullets). The context shows he believes the revolutionists have already threatened force ("the bear reached out his paws to crush us"). Therefore, continuing verbal debate is pointless. This conclusion is directly supported.

Option C is incorrect. The passage describes Wickson as "cool" and "coldly and dispassionately." He shows no sign of secret fear. He acknowledges Ernest's skill ("outgeneralled") but does not suggest that Ernest's logic is unanswerable. In fact, he refuses to engage with the logic at all, not because he cannot refute it, but because he believes force supersedes argument. Fear is not evidenced.

Option D is incorrect. This overgeneralizes. Wickson is responding to a specific threat from a specific revolutionary movement. He does not make a universal claim that speeches never change wealth distribution. He even later hears Ernest mention ballots without denying that ballots exist as a method. He simply rejects words in this confrontation because he believes force is the only appropriate answer.

questions.questionHtml: Ernest responds to Wickson's speech by saying: "I am answered. It is the only answer that could be given." Which unstated assumption does Ernest rely on most directly in this response?

options.A: That the capitalist class has already decided to use violence regardless of what the working class does.
options.B: That the working class is morally superior because it appeals to justice rather than force.
options.C: That Mr. Wickson's argument is logically flawed but politically effective.
options.D: That no peaceful or democratic method can succeed because the ruling class will never accept electoral defeat.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

Option A is incorrect. While Wickson does threaten violence, Ernest's assumption is not simply "they have already decided." That is stated directly, not unstated. The deeper assumption is that because they have decided on violence, any peaceful method (like elections) will fail. Option A captures only the surface, not the assumption driving Ernest's conclusion that this was "the only answer."

Option B is incorrect. Ernest does believe in moral superiority (he calls their hearts "hard"), but that is not the assumption that leads him to say "it is the only answer." He is making a pragmatic observation about what the capitalist class will accept, not a moral claim about who is better. This option confuses his values with his reasoning.

Option C is incorrect. Ernest never says Wickson's argument is logically flawed. In fact, he says "I am answered," which indicates acceptance of the argument as valid given the premises. Claiming it is flawed would contradict his direct statement. This option is not supported.

Option D is correct. Ernest immediately follows his response by saying that the working class has preached power "by the power of our ballots" — implying that they hoped for peaceful change. But Wickson's answer of force shows that even if workers win elections, the capitalists will refuse to hand over power. Ernest's unstated assumption is that the ruling class will never voluntarily accept a democratic defeat; therefore, force is the only possible language. This is the assumption that makes Wickson's answer "the only one that could be given."

questions.questionHtml: Mr. Wickson argues: "As for the host of labor, it has been in the dirt since history began ... and in the dirt it shall remain so long as I and mine ... have the power." Which of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the validity of his conclusion?

options.A: That in some past societies, ruling classes granted labor major political rights, yet remained in power for centuries.
options.B: That past ruling classes who relied solely on military force were eventually overthrown by organized rebellions.
options.C: That the working class in some countries has achieved significant economic gains without changing the basic class structure.
options.D: That Wickson's own class has occasionally made temporary compromises with labor leaders to avoid strikes.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

Option A is incorrect. This actually strengthens Wickson's argument, or at least does not weaken it. If ruling classes can grant rights and still remain in power for centuries, that supports his claim that labor "shall remain in the dirt" (i.e., under capitalist control). It does not challenge the idea that power keeps labor down. This is a clever wrong answer because it sounds like progress for labor, but Wickson could use it as evidence that concessions don't threaten class power.

Option B is correct. Wickson's conclusion rests on the assumption that because he and his class "have the power" now, labor will remain in the dirt forever. Historical evidence that ruling classes relying only on force were eventually overthrown directly challenges that assumption. If power based solely on force is historically unstable, then his prediction is likely wrong. This seriously weakens his argument.

Option C is incorrect. This seems to weaken at first, but Wickson could argue that economic gains without changing the class structure are exactly what he expects — they leave power in his hands. The claim "labor shall remain in the dirt" refers to structural subordination, not absolute poverty. Economic gains within capitalism do not disprove his conclusion. This is a plausible but ultimately incorrect choice.

Option D is incorrect. Temporary compromises to avoid strikes do not threaten Wickson's overall power. In fact, shrewd rulers often use concessions to preserve their rule. This evidence would not weaken his claim that labor remains in the dirt as long as his class has power; it might even show how power is maintained through tactical compromises. A student might think compromise weakens his hardline stance, but the argument's core is about ultimate power, not tactical flexibility.

questions.questionHtml: Based on the entire exchange, which generalization about the nature of their conflict is most strongly supported?

options.A: Both sides believe that the ultimate basis of political authority is superior moral righteousness.
options.B: Both sides agree that violence is inevitable but disagree about which side would start it.
options.C: Both sides accept that power (force) is the final arbiter, though they differ on how to organize that power.
options.D: Both sides reject the possibility of compromise but disagree on whether elections are a useful tool.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

Option A is incorrect. Wickson explicitly rejects morality ("intruding ethics"). He says "Not God, not Mammon, but Power." Ernest does appeal to justice ("right, justice, humanity"), but he concludes that those appeals will not work and that power is what matters. The generalization that both base authority on morality is false.

Option B is incorrect. They do not merely agree that violence is inevitable; they actively embrace it as the appropriate answer. Also, the passage does not show them disagreeing on who would start it — each implies the other side will. More importantly, this option misses the central point: they agree on the role of force as the final arbiter, not just its inevitability.

Option C is correct. Wickson states that power is "the king of words" and promises machine-guns. Ernest replies, "I am answered ... Power it shall be ... in roar of shell and shrapnel." Both conclude that force will ultimately decide. They differ on method (Wickson trusts existing state power; Ernest hopes to win power through ballots first, then force if necessary), but both accept that power/force is the final arbiter. This generalization is strongly supported.

Option D is incorrect. Ernest does not reject compromise entirely; he offers elections as a peaceful method. Wickson rejects compromise entirely. Therefore, they do not share this generalization. Also, the passage's main shared conclusion is about power, not about elections or compromise.

questions.questionHtml: Based on the passage, which conclusion about Mr. Thornton's position is best supported?

options.A: He believes that workers are naturally childlike, but he has no responsibility for keeping them that way; however, their childlike condition still justifies his absolute authority during work hours.
options.B: He argues that because workers are independent outside of work, he has no right to interfere with them at any time, even during working hours.
options.C: He claims that his power over workers is purely economic and that he would prefer a republic where no one has authority over anyone else.
options.D: He thinks that strikes are the only legitimate way for workers to express their independence, and he welcomes them as a check on his own power.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

A is correct: Thornton explicitly says workers are "in the condition of children," denies masters make them so, and then concludes "despotism is the best kind of government for them" during work hours. This is a nuanced conclusion: he accepts the childlike state as a given, not his fault, but still uses it to justify autocracy.

Why distractors are wrong:

B is contradicted – he asserts authority during work hours, just not outside.

C is false – he rejects a republic for "our present state" and grounds his authority in more than economics (he calls himself an autocrat by nature of the relationship).

D is false – he calls strikers "fools" and says he will not alter "one jot," so he does not welcome strikes as a check.

questions.questionHtml: Margaret tells the story of the Nuremberg man and his isolated son. How does Mr. Thornton implicitly argue that this analogy is not relevant to his own situation?

options.A: He points out that the father in the story actively kept his son ignorant, whereas Thornton repeatedly states that masters do not cause the workers' childlike condition.
options.B: He changes the subject to his appointment at eight o'clock, implying that theoretical stories are useless in practical business matters.
options.C: He argues that the Nuremberg father was a single rich man living alone, while a mill owner is part of a whole system of commerce and society.
options.D: He claims that the son in the story was kept ignorant for forty years, but workers in Milton are only under the master's authority for a few hours a day.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

A is correct: The key flaw in Margaret's analogy is that the father deliberately created and maintained ignorance. Thornton's whole defense rests on denying that masters make workers childlike ("I deny that we ... have anything to do with the making or keeping them so"). The analogy fails because it assumes a causal role that Thornton rejects. This is implicit – he never says "your analogy is wrong because X," but his earlier denial directly undermines it.

Why distractors are wrong:

B is a surface reading – he mentions the appointment before her story is finished, but that's a social excuse, not an implicit argument against the analogy.

C is never stated or implied – he does not contrast "single rich man" with "system of commerce."

D is a plausible distractor – he does mention the limited hours ("less than a third of their lives"), but that appears before the Nuremberg story, not in direct response to it. His main rebuttal to the analogy is the causation point, not the duration point.

questions.questionHtml: Mr. Thornton asks: "Have I any right to obtrude my views ... merely because he has labour to sell and I capital to buy?" Margaret replies: "Not in the least ... but because you are a man, dealing with a set of men over whom you have ... immense power." Which of the following is an assumption that Margaret's reply depends on, but that Mr. Thornton would likely reject?

options.A: Economic transactions between a buyer and a seller create no moral obligations beyond the terms of the contract.
options.B: A person's character is entirely determined by their social class and economic role.
options.C: The fact of having power over others, regardless of how that power was obtained, creates a moral duty that overrides the principle of non-interference.
options.D: Workers in Darkshire do not actually value their independence as much as they claim to.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

C is correct: Margaret shifts from the economic frame ("labour for capital") to a power frame ("immense power"). For her argument to work, she must assume that power itself – not its origin or the contract – generates moral responsibility. Thornton rejects this because he believes the relationship ends when work hours end, and he values his own independence too much to accept interference. C is the hidden assumption that divides them.

Why distractors are wrong:

A is the opposite of Margaret's view – she is adding obligations beyond the contract. Thornton might agree with A, but Margaret does not. This is a trick: the question asks for an assumption Margaret depends on that Thornton would reject. A is rejected by Margaret, so it cannot be her assumption.

B is extreme and not supported – Margaret never says character is entirely determined by class.

D is not stated or implied – she never questions whether workers value independence. Thornton asserts they do, and she does not contradict that.

questions.questionHtml: The writer uses the hypothetical example of a person viewing Earth before life emerged. What conclusion does the writer intend readers to draw from this example?

options.A: Because past humans incorrectly thought consciousness impossible on a lifeless planet, present humans are likely incorrect to think mechanical consciousness impossible.
options.B: Human ignorance of physical science in the past proves that consciousness is not a product of physical processes but a mysterious addition from outside nature.
options.C: The fact that consciousness eventually appeared proves that machines will inevitably develop a form of consciousness identical to human consciousness.
options.D: Early Earth was actually more hospitable to life than it appeared, so we should be optimistic about machines even when they seem lifeless.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

A is correct: The writer sets up a historical pattern: someone in the past would have declared consciousness impossible on a lifeless Earth, yet consciousness developed. The implied conclusion is that we might be making the same mistake today about machines. This is an argument from analogy: past error suggests present error is likely.

B is incorrect: Option B claims that past ignorance proves consciousness is non-physical. But the writer never says that. In fact, the writer later asks whether even "spiritual" things are mechanical. B reverses the writer's actual position.

C is incorrect: C overstates the claim. The writer never says machine consciousness will be identical to human consciousness; he says a "new phase of mind" could arise, as different as animal from vegetable. C adds the word "identical," which is not supported.

D is incorrect: D misinterprets the hypothetical. The writer does not say early Earth was secretly hospitable; he says it appeared impossible for life. The point is about the limits of human perception, not about actual conditions.

questions.questionHtml: The writer argues that a potato has "low cunning" and "knows perfectly well what it wants" because it sends shoots toward light. Which of the following is an unstated assumption necessary for this claim to be valid?

options.A: Any organism that can move toward a resource must possess the same kind of consciousness as a human being who shops for food.
options.B: The potato's ability to distinguish light from darkness requires a brain or at least a simple nervous system.
options.C: Purposeful behavior can exist without subjective self-awareness or the ability to feel pleasure and pain.
options.D: Potatoes that fail to grow toward light are less intelligent than those that succeed, proving natural selection favors conscious potatoes.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

A is incorrect: A demands that potato consciousness be the same as human consciousness when shopping. The writer never makes such an extreme claim; he only suggests that the potato's behavior shares some features with purposeful human action, not that they are identical.

B is incorrect: B directly contradicts the writer's purpose. He is arguing against the idea that a brain or nervous system is needed for intelligent-seeming behavior. If B were assumed, the potato example would not support his argument.

C is correct: For the potato's goal-directed behavior to count as "cunning" or "knowing," the writer must assume that such behavior does not require subjective self-awareness, language, or emotion. Without this assumption, the potato example would fail to challenge the line between mechanical and conscious action.

D is incorrect: D introduces claims about natural selection, intelligence rankings, and consciousness in potatoes that are never mentioned in the passage. It is an unsupported extension of the writer's point.

questions.questionHtml: The writer asks: "If this is unconsciousness, where is the use of consciousness?" (referring to the carnivorous plant). What can be reasonably inferred about the writer's position from this rhetorical question?

options.A: The writer believes consciousness serves no practical function because plants can survive and reproduce without it.
options.B: The writer is suggesting that if a plant can act in its own interest without consciousness, then consciousness may not be necessary for intelligent-seeming behavior.
options.C: The writer concludes that the plant must actually be conscious because otherwise its selective feeding would be impossible to explain.
options.D: The writer argues that consciousness is overrated and that humans would be better off if they acted more mechanically like plants.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

A is incorrect: A mistakes a rhetorical challenge for a direct assertion. The writer does not state that consciousness has no function; he is asking readers to rethink what consciousness is for. A takes the question too literally as a conclusion.

B is correct: The writer's rhetorical question challenges the reader: if we call the plant "unconscious" yet it acts in its own interest, then what purpose does consciousness serve? The implied position is that consciousness may not be necessary for intelligent behavior. The writer is raising doubt, not making a flat statement.

C is incorrect: C goes beyond what the writer claims. He does not conclude the plant is definitely conscious; he uses the example to blur the boundary. C turns a skeptical inquiry into a dogmatic statement.

D is incorrect: D adds a prescriptive claim (humans "would be better off" acting mechanically) that the passage never makes. The writer is making a philosophical point about definitions, not giving advice on human behavior.

questions.questionHtml: The writer claims that human thoughts and emotions might be "nothing but disturbances of equilibrium in an infinite series of levers." Which statement best evaluates whether the writer provides sufficient evidence for this claim in the passage?

options.A: The evidence is sufficient because the writer shows that potato behavior, which seems purposeful, can be explained mechanically, so human thought likely follows the same pattern.
options.B: The evidence is insufficient because the writer only speculates about levers and molecular action without providing any experimental data or scientific studies.
options.C: The evidence is sufficient because the writer's rhetorical questions force the reader to admit that no clear line separates mechanical from conscious action.
options.D: The evidence is insufficient because even if potato actions are mechanical, that does not logically prove that human spiritual experiences are also mechanical—it only raises a possibility.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

A is incorrect: A wrongly treats an analogy as sufficient proof. The writer shows a similarity between potato behavior and human behavior, but similarity does not equal causation or identity. This option confuses plausibility with logical sufficiency.

B is incorrect: B imposes an external standard (experimental data) that the passage never claims to meet. The GED does not require scientific experiments for philosophical arguments; it asks whether the reasoning within the text supports the claim. B is a common trap but too strict for this context.

C is incorrect: C confuses rhetorical force with evidence. The writer's questions may challenge the reader's assumptions, but challenges are not the same as proof. Just because a question makes you think does not mean it provides sufficient evidence for a claim.

D is correct: The writer raises the possibility that human spiritual experiences might be mechanical ("disturbances of equilibrium... levers"). However, the only evidence offered is the potato analogy and rhetorical questions. Showing that potato actions could be mechanical does not logically prove that human thoughts are mechanical. The evidence is suggestive but insufficient to reach a firm conclusion.

questions.questionHtml: Based on Dr. Leete's statements about nineteenth-century cities, which conclusion is best supported?

options.A: The poverty caused by the nineteenth-century industrial system made it impossible for cities to be magnificent.
options.B: If a society values private luxury, it will never produce any public art or architecture.
options.C: The economic and social organization of a society affects whether wealth is used for shared or private benefit.
options.D: Dr. Leete believes that the twentieth century has eliminated poverty completely.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

Option A is incorrect. Dr. Leete mentions both poverty and excessive individualism as reasons cities were shabby. He does not claim poverty alone was sufficient. The passage says poverty "would not have given you the means," but it also says individualism "was inconsistent with much public spirit." So A oversimplifies his argument.

Option B is incorrect. This is too absolute. Dr. Leete only compares two specific eras. He does not argue that valuing private luxury always prevents any public art. The word "never" makes this unsupported.

Option C is correct. Dr. Leete directly links the "extraordinary industrial system" and "excessive individualism" to a lack of public wealth, and contrasts with the twentieth-century system where surplus wealth goes to public adornment. The conclusion that economic/social organization affects how wealth is directed (shared vs. private) is strongly supported.

Option D is incorrect. Dr. Leete praises the twentieth century's use of surplus wealth for city adornment, but he never claims poverty has been completely eliminated. The passage does not provide evidence for that claim.

questions.questionHtml: The narrator says that Edith Leete combines "feminine softness and delicacy" with "health and abounding physical vitality too often lacking in the maidens with whom alone I could compare her." What can be reasonably inferred?

options.A: In the nineteenth century, women who had feminine softness rarely had good health because the two were considered opposites.
options.B: The narrator finds Edith less attractive than the women of his own time because she is too robust.
options.C: The women the narrator knew in the nineteenth century typically had softness and delicacy but often lacked the level of physical vitality Edith has.
options.D: Physical vitality was the only quality that made Edith beautiful; her facial features were unimportant.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

Option A is incorrect. The narrator says health was "too often lacking," but he does not say it was rare or that the two were considered opposites. He also does not give a reason why it was lacking. This option adds a cause-and-effect claim not found in the text.

Option B is incorrect. The narrator explicitly calls Edith "the most beautiful girl I had ever seen." He admires her combination of traits. He does not find her less attractive.

Option C is correct. The narrator compares Edith to "the maidens with whom alone I could compare her" - meaning women of his own time. He says those maidens "too often lacked" the health and vitality that Edith has, while still having softness and delicacy. This inference is directly supported.

Option D is incorrect. The narrator says that even if her face lacked special charms, her figure would still make her a beauty. But he does not say her face was unimportant; he actually describes her face as bewitching. This option misreads the text.

questions.questionHtml: In the footnote, the narrator argues that his new surroundings gave him "next to nothing to suggest what had befallen me" (i.e., that he had traveled a century into the future). Which evidence best supports this claim?

options.A: The complete absence of chimneys and smoke in the twentieth-century city.
options.B: Dr. Leete had to physically restrain the narrator from attacking him on the rooftop.
options.C: The narrator could not discover the source of the artificial light inside the house.
options.D: Changes in speech, dress, and furniture were no greater than normal fashion shifts within one generation.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

Option A is incorrect. The absence of chimneys and smoke is a major physical difference. It would actually suggest that something extraordinary had happened, not that things felt normal. This evidence weakens the footnote's claim.

Option B is incorrect. The narrator's near-attack shows he was disoriented and alarmed, which contradicts the idea that his surroundings felt familiar. This also undermines the claim.

Option C is incorrect. Not knowing the source of light is a mystery that highlights the strangeness of the new world. It would make the narrator more aware that something unusual had occurred, not less.

Option D is correct. The narrator says language, dress, and furniture changed less than normal fashion changes within a single generation. This means everyday life looked and sounded almost the same as in his own time. That directly supports the claim that his surroundings gave him little reason to suspect a century-long leap.

questions.questionHtml: Dr. Leete argues that nineteenth-century wealth went to private luxury, while twentieth-century surplus wealth goes to city adornment "which all enjoy in equal degree." Which unstated assumption is necessary for him to imply that the twentieth-century system is better in this respect?

options.A: Private luxury is always wasteful, and public adornment is always beneficial.
options.B: The main measure of a society's success is how much money is spent on buildings.
options.C: Surplus wealth should be used for things that provide shared enjoyment rather than private enjoyment.
options.D: The nineteenth century had no public adornment whatsoever.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

Option A is incorrect. Dr. Leete does not say private luxury is always wasteful or that public adornment is always beneficial. He is comparing two specific systems. The word "always" makes this assumption too extreme and not necessary for his argument.

Option B is incorrect. He praises city adornment as one popular destination of surplus wealth, but he never claims it is the main measure of a society's success. This misrepresents his point.

Option C is correct. For Dr. Leete to prefer the twentieth-century approach, he must assume that using surplus wealth for shared enjoyment (public adornment) is better than using it for private luxury. This value judgment is not stated but is necessary to his implied superiority claim.

Option D is incorrect. He says the old cities were "shabby" and wealth went to private luxury, but he does not claim there was no public adornment at all. This absolute assumption is not needed; his argument only requires that public adornment was much less, not zero.

questions.questionHtml: Based on Dr. Maynard's testimony, what can most reasonably be inferred about the victim's state of mind or awareness just before the shooting?

options.A: The victim was asleep and never woke up.
options.B: The victim was anxious and trying to escape.
options.C: The victim likely recognized the approaching person and did not feel threatened.
options.D: The victim was expecting a stranger and was caught off guard.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

Option A is incorrect. The passage states the victim was seated and engaged in some occupation (likely writing). There is no mention of sleep. The bullet entered the back of the head while he was sitting upright or leaning forward – not lying down asleep.

Option B is incorrect. Dr. Maynard explicitly says the victim "had made no effort to raise or turn his head." An anxious person trying to escape would likely move, turn around, or at least tense up. The evidence shows no such effort.

Option C is correct. The passage directly concludes that "the footstep was an accustomed one, and the presence of its possessor in the room either known or expected." An accustomed footstep means the victim had heard that person walk up behind him many times before. Not feeling threatened is implied by the lack of any defensive movement.

Option D is incorrect. While the victim may have "expected" someone, the key word "accustomed" tells us the person was familiar, not a stranger. Expecting a stranger would usually cause a person to turn around or at least be alert. The evidence points to familiarity, not surprise by an unknown person.

questions.questionHtml: Dr. Maynard argues that the victim's head was bent forward at the time of the shooting. Which of the following, if true, would most weaken his conclusion?

options.A: The chair in which the victim was sitting had a very low back, forcing him to sit unusually erect.
options.B: The bullet was later determined to have been fired from a distance of more than ten feet.
options.C: A separate witness testified that the victim was left-handed, but the bullet entered the right side of the skull.
options.D: The pistol used in the murder was found to have been held at a 90-degree angle to the floor.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

Option A is correct. Dr. Maynard's conclusion that the head was bent forward depends on the angle of entry being 45 degrees. He compares a seated erect head (which would require the pistol to be held "very low down" and in "a peculiar position") to a bent-forward head (which makes the angle easy). If the chair forced the victim to sit unusually erect, then even a bent-forward posture might be impossible. This would weaken the doctor's preferred explanation and make the "peculiar position" of the gun more likely, but the question asks what would weaken his conclusion that the head was bent forward. A chair preventing forward bending directly challenges that claim.

Option B is incorrect. The passage already states the shot came from "three or four feet distant." A greater distance would not change the angle analysis; the same geometric relationship between head posture and gun position holds regardless of distance (within reasonable range). In fact, a longer distance might make the angle even harder to achieve with a seated erect head, but it doesn't directly weaken the claim that the head was bent forward. More importantly, the doctor's conclusion about head posture is based on angle, not distance.

Option C is incorrect. The passage does not specify which side of the skull the bullet entered, only that it entered the "back of the head." Handedness of the victim has no logical connection to whether his head was bent forward. The shooter's handedness might matter, but the victim's handedness is irrelevant to head posture. This option tries to distract with an irrelevant detail.

Option D is incorrect. A 90-degree angle to the floor would mean the pistol was held perfectly horizontal. The doctor describes a scenario where the pistol is held naturally with the elbow bent - which is not 90 degrees. But this does not weaken the conclusion that the victim's head was bent forward; it would only suggest the shooter held the gun in an unusual way. The doctor's conclusion about the victim's posture does not depend on the shooter's exact grip angle, only on the bullet's entry angle relative to the victim.

questions.questionHtml: Dr. Maynard notes the bullet was "small" and "from a rifled barrel... especially liable to deflections." How does this information support his claim that the victim made no effort to move his head?

options.A: Because a small bullet travels faster than a large one, giving the victim no time to react.
options.B: Because a rifled bullet is less accurate, so the shooter had to be extremely close, making movement pointless.
options.C: Because the bullet's tendency to deflect means any sudden head movement would likely have altered its path, but the wound shows a clean, undeflected trajectory.
options.D: Because small, rifled bullets are designed to tumble on impact, which would have caused a larger wound if the victim had moved.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

Option A is incorrect. The passage does not mention bullet speed or reaction time. Even if a small bullet travels fast, that would not require the victim to be motionless – he could still have begun to move before the bullet arrived. The doctor's reasoning is different: he focuses on deflection, not speed.

Option B is incorrect. Rifling (spiral grooves inside the barrel) actually makes a bullet more accurate, not less. The passage says the bullet is "liable to deflections while passing through bones" – that is about what happens inside the body, not about accuracy in flight. This option contains a factual misunderstanding not present in the text.

Option C is correct. The doctor's logic: because the bullet is especially prone to deflections when passing through tissue and bone, any movement of the victim's head would likely have pushed the bullet off a straight path. The fact that the bullet followed a clean, undeflected trajectory (he extracted it in one piece and described the angle precisely) shows the head was still at the moment of impact. This is a careful inference.

Option D is incorrect. The passage never states that rifled bullets "tumble on impact." Some bullets do, but the doctor only mentions "deflections" (changes in direction), not tumbling or a larger wound. This option adds invented details not supported by the testimony.

questions.questionHtml: At the end of the passage, the coroner writes a note and sends an officer who immediately takes a cab toward Broadway. Based on the sequence of events, which of the following inferences is least supported by the passage?

options.A: The officer's departure suggests the coroner is actively investigating a new lead.
options.B: The officer likely knows the purpose of his errand, as he looks at the note "knowingly."
options.C: The coroner's action is likely related to the bullet he had just examined.
options.D: The coroner has concluded that one of Mr. Leavenworth's nieces is responsible for the murder.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

Option A is supported. The officer leaves "hastily" and takes a cab. This shows urgency and purpose, which strongly suggests the coroner is following up on something – a new investigative lead. This is a logical inference.

Option B is supported. The passage says the officer looked at the slip "for an instant knowingly." This directly indicates he understood the note's meaning. This is explicitly supported.

Option C is supported. The coroner had just picked up the bullet, rolled it between his fingers, and then wrote the note. The timing strongly links the note to the bullet. This is a reasonable inference.

Option D is the least supported (correct answer). The narrator earlier had a personal "fancy" that the nieces looked like a painting, but that is pure imagination, not evidence. The coroner never mentions the nieces, and there is no link between the bullet examination and any specific suspect. The passage provides no factual basis for concluding the coroner blames a niece. This inference has no support in the text.
